<reason>B's strongest move was flipping A's equity argument: B showed that categorical sequencing itself imposes equity costs on disabled and rural students who have ready, cheap, need-matched digital options (adaptive coding, text-to-speech, switch-access tools) while comparable physical/arts remedies require staffing pipelines, certified aides, and equipment that under-resourced districts don't have. A never fully answered this specific mechanism, instead repeatedly reasserting that physical/embodied experience is "categorically irreplaceable" without engaging why a child whose actual unmet need is belonging or creativity should wait behind an unrelated construction timeline. B also successfully exploited A's own concession ("some digital expansion will wait") to show the softened "meaningful increase, not full completion" framing still enacts the harmful category freeze. B's late refinement in Rebuttal 2 — match remedy to specific need, use speed only among options that meet that need — cleanly answered A's Q2 pressure question and resolved the earlier tension in B's case, making B's triage principle more coherent by the end than A's category-based rule. A's closing catch about budget competition was a fair jab but not decisive enough to offset B's more granular, unanswered mechanism-level attacks. Both sides followed the Q/A format correctly, but B's answers did more actual work.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's Rebuttal 2 (B4.1–B4.5), refining the triage rule to "match remedy to specific need, use speed only among options that can meet it" — this directly neutralized A's Q2 pressure question about physically-needy children being left behind, while A's parallel rebuttal never found an equally clean answer to the disabled/rural off-the-shelf digital tool example.</best_rebuttal>
